EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) at the rounding thresholds that translate minority population share into the number of reserved seats.  

Why appropriate:  
• The institutional rule generates deterministic, discontinuous jumps in representation that are as‐good‐as-random for states whose minority share is infinitesimally on either side of a threshold.  
• States cannot finely manipulate Census-measured population shares, so near each threshold assignment is plausibly exogenous.  
• RDD exploits cross-sectional variation in every census year; combining multiple censuses/elections provides additional power while preserving the local RD logic.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_sct = 1{SC (or ST) population share ≥ cutoff_j} where cutoff_j is the share that triggers j + 1 vs. j reserved seats. In practice we estimate the impact of one additional reserved seat.  

Control group  
States just below a threshold (j seats) serve as counterfactual for states just above the same threshold (j + 1 seats).  

Timing  
Treatment is “in force” for the entire legislative term that follows the census that set the quotas. (E.g., 1971 Census → quotas used for 1974–1981 elections.) The running variable and treatment are therefore treated as time-constant between censuses.  

Running variable & cutoffs  
Running variable X_it = SC (or ST) share in state i in census c that applies to year-t elections. Each threshold k is (k + ½)/TotalSeats_i. Because total seats differ across states the actual cutoff is state-specific; we express the running variable in “seat-share” units:  
z_it = TotalSeats_i × SCshare_it − round(TotalSeats_i × SCshare_it).  
A jump occurs at z_it = +½ seat. We center z_it so that 0 is the threshold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of the seat jump, redistributive policies would vary smoothly in minority share.  
- Plausible: policy formulas are not pegged to the same rounding rule.  

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable: States cannot strategically influence their recorded SC/ST shares at the census to gain/lose one seat.  
- Plausible: Census is conducted by the federal Statistical Office; incentive is weak because one seat out of 150 has small electoral value.  

A3. The only policy discontinuity at the threshold is the change in reserved seats.  
- Plausible: Other constitutional provisions (e.g., job reservations) depend on all-India rules and do not jump at state-level population thresholds.  

A4. Stable unit treatment value: One state’s extra reserved seat does not directly affect another’s redistributive spending in the immediate census cycle.  
- Reasonable for within-state spending outcomes.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation or mis-measurement of caste/tribe shares.  
  • Test: McCrary density test at each threshold.  
  • Mitigate: show no bunching; replicate using alternative data (sample surveys).  

T2. Other policies or transfers keyed to SC/ST share could also be discontinuous.  
  • Collect data on central grants, poverty programs, etc.; show no jumps.  
  • Run placebo RDs on outcomes unrelated to representation (e.g., road length).  

T3. Heterogeneous total assembly size means bandwidth in share units differs by state.  
  • Estimate in seat-share space; cluster by state; run state-fixed-effect RD with interacted polynomials so local fit is state-specific.  
  • Repeat with normalized share (X – cutoff) × total seats to confirm robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages ----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data
library(fixest)        # regressions
library(rdrobust)      # RD inference
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data ----------------------------------------------------------
d <- fread("state_econ_scst_1960_1992.csv")   # assume one row per state-year

# 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------
# Running variable in seat units
d[, seats_needed := total_seats * sc_share]              # example for SC
d[, seat_frac := seats_needed - round(seats_needed)]     # distance to integer
d[, rd_running := seat_frac]                             # 0.5 jumps to +1 seat
# Center at threshold: shift so 0 = 0.5 seat
d[, rd_running := rd_running - 0.5]

# Treatment: one extra reserved seat (sharp RD)
d[, treat := as.integer(rd_running >= 0)]

# Outcomes
yvars <- c("sc_welfare_spend_pc", "minority_job_quota", 
           "land_reform_index", "public_sector_scst_share")

# 3. Main specification (local linear RD) -------------------------
main_out <- list()
for (y in yvars) {
  main_out[[y]] <- rdrobust(y = d[[y]],
                            x = d$rd_running,
                            covs = d[, .(log_gdp, log_pop, urban_share,
                                         ruling_party_left, total_seats)],
                            bwselect = "mserd")
}

# 4. Robustness check: different bandwidth & donut -----------------
d_donut <- d[abs(rd_running) > 0.01]    # drop ±0.01 seat around cutoff
robust_out <- rdrobust(y = d_donut$sc_welfare_spend_pc,
                       x = d_donut$rd_running,
                       bw = 0.25)       # fixed 0.25-seat bandwidth

# 5. Plot RD -------------------------------------------------------
ggplot(d, aes(rd_running, sc_welfare_spend_pc))+
  geom_point(alpha=.4)+
  geom_smooth(method="loess", span=.4)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype="dashed")+
  labs(x = "Distance to seat threshold (seats)",
       y = "Per-capita SC welfare spending")

```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior: One additional reserved SC seat (≈0.7 % increase in legislators) will raise SC-targeted welfare spending by roughly 5–10 % and modestly increase minority share in public employment. Land reforms and job quotas should move in the pro-minority direction but effect sizes are likely smaller (≤3 % absolute change) because implementation is slower.  

Theory: Political representation increases the bargaining weight of the minority; hence redistributive policies toward that group increase.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Density continuity at cutoff (McCrary test) .................. 1  
C2: Covariate balance at cutoff .................................. 1  
C3: No other policy discontinuities at cutoff .................... 0.8  
C4: Functional form/bandwidth robustness demonstrated ............ 1  
C5: Sufficient observations near each threshold .................. 0.7  

Overall: 4.5 / 5 ≈ strong internal validity conditional on passing diagnostic tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
END
